title: The Empty Tomb and the Risen Lord
summary: Early on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene finds the tomb open; Peter and the beloved disciple run to it and find the grave clothes lying there. The risen Jesus meets Mary in the garden, then appears to the disciples behind locked doors, breathes the Holy Spirit on them, and sends them out. A week later he meets the doubting Thomas, who confesses him as Lord and God, and John states the purpose of his book.
story:
The body of Jesus was laid in a garden tomb as the Sabbath began (19:41-42). Now, on the first day of the week, the story that seemed ended begins again. The Gospel that opened with “In the beginning” (1:1) shows a new beginning in a garden, with the risen Lord breathing new life into his followers as God once breathed life into the first human. The chapter moves from absence to presence: an empty tomb, then a voice calling Mary by name, then Jesus standing among frightened disciples, then a doubter invited to touch his wounds. It also moves from sight to faith, closing with a blessing on those who will believe without seeing, which includes every later reader of the book.

The chapter fulfills promises made at the supper. Jesus had said he would not leave his disciples as orphans but would come to them (14:18), that their grief would turn to joy (16:20-22), that he would give them his peace (14:27), and that he would send the Spirit (16:7). Each of those promises is kept here. Chapter 21 will follow as an epilogue, but verses 30 and 31 are the Gospel's formal conclusion, telling the reader why everything in the book was written.
historical:
The resurrection of Jesus is the church's first-order confession, and the Gospels present it as an event in history, not as a symbol or a private experience. The earliest written summary is not in the Gospels but in Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, written around AD 53 to 55, where Paul passes on a tradition he had himself received: that Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas (Peter), to the Twelve, to more than five hundred at once, to James, to all the apostles, and last to Paul (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). Many scholars think Paul received this summary within a few years of the events, perhaps when he visited Peter and James in Jerusalem about three years after his conversion (Galatians 1:18-19).

Jewish hope in the first century already included resurrection, but as an event at the end of history for all the righteous together (Daniel 12:2, 2 Maccabees 7; the Pharisees' belief in Acts 23:8 and Josephus, Jewish War 2.163). No Jewish group expected a single person, let alone a crucified messiah, to be raised bodily in the middle of history. N. T. Wright (The Resurrection of the Son of God, 2003) argued at length that the disciples' claim cannot be explained as borrowed from existing expectation, and that the combination of an empty tomb and appearances best explains how the claim arose. Others read the same evidence differently. Gerd Lüdemann (The Resurrection of Jesus, 1994) proposed that Peter, burdened by guilt over his denial, had a vision of Jesus that spread to others; Dale Allison (Resurrecting Jesus, 2005) judged the empty tomb and the appearances both likely historical while leaving open how they should be explained; and the Orthodox Jewish scholar Pinchas Lapide (The Resurrection of Jesus: A Jewish Perspective, 1983) concluded that the resurrection was a real event while denying that it made Jesus the Messiah.

Several details of John's account touch known history. The first witnesses are women, led by Mary Magdalene, from the fishing town of Magdala on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, where excavations since 2009 have uncovered a first-century synagogue. Women's testimony carried little weight in a Jewish court: Josephus says it was not accepted (Antiquities 4.219), and the Mishnah exempts women from the oath of testimony (m. Shevuot 4:1). In the second century the pagan critic Celsus mocked the resurrection as resting on the word of a half-frantic woman (Origen, Against Celsus 2.55). A story invented to persuade would hardly have begun this way. The earliest alternative explanation, that the disciples stole the body, is reported in Matthew 28:11-15 and again by Justin Martyr around AD 160 (Dialogue with Trypho 108); both presuppose that the tomb was empty. Tertullian mockingly mentions another, that the gardener removed the body so that visitors would not trample his lettuces (On the Spectacles 30), and a gardener who hides the body appears in the medieval Jewish parody Toledot Yeshu.
cultural:
The first day of the week, Sunday, began for Jews at sundown on Saturday, and Mary comes while it is still dark, as soon as the Sabbath rest allowed. The tombs of the well-to-do around Jerusalem were chambers cut into rock, entered by a low doorway that one had to stoop to look through (verses 5 and 11), with burial benches or niches inside. The entrance was closed with a blocking stone. Amos Kloner, who studied more than nine hundred tombs of the period around Jerusalem, found that over ninety-eight percent were closed with square stones pulled into place; round rolling stones were rare and belonged to the wealthiest families (Biblical Archaeology Review, 1999). Mark says the stone had been rolled away (Mark 16:4); John says only that it had been removed, which fits either kind.

The linen cloths lying in place and the face cloth (soudarion, from the Latin sudarium, the same word used for Lazarus in 11:44) folded or rolled up by itself suggest an orderly scene. John Chrysostom argued that the body had been bound with a large quantity of myrrh, which glues linen to the body, so that a thief would never have taken the time to unwrap it (Homilies on John 85). Mary's address to Jesus, Rabboni (verse 16), is an Aramaic form of rabbi, found also in Mark 10:51; John translates it as Teacher. When she recognizes him, she evidently takes hold of him, and Jesus' words mean something like stop clinging to me, not do not touch me at all; Matthew says the women took hold of his feet (Matthew 28:9).

“Peace be with you” (verses 19, 21, and 26) was the everyday Jewish greeting, shalom, but on the lips of the risen Jesus, spoken to men who had abandoned him, it carries the full weight of reconciliation and fulfills his promise of peace (14:27, 16:33). The disciples meet behind locked doors for fear of the Jewish authorities, whose officers had arrested their master three days before. Eight days later (verse 26), counted inclusively in the ancient way, is again the first day of the week; the church's weekly gathering on the Lord's Day (Revelation 1:10; Didache 14:1; Justin Martyr, First Apology 67) grew from these Sunday meetings with the risen Lord.

Thomas's other name, Didymus, is the Greek word for twin, as Thomas comes from the Aramaic word for twin. His confession, “My Lord and my God!” (verse 28), joins the two titles the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel's God, and a psalm uses almost the same pairing in prayer (Psalm 35:23, Psalm 34:23 in the Greek numbering). Later in the first century the emperor Domitian (AD 81 to 96), Suetonius says, had his letters begin with the formula our Lord and God (Domitian 13); if John wrote during or after his reign, as many think, the confession would have had a sharp edge for its first readers.
literary:
The chapter is built in four scenes: the empty tomb (verses 1 to 10), Mary and Jesus (11 to 18), the disciples on Easter evening (19 to 23), and Thomas a week later (24 to 29), followed by the statement of purpose (30 and 31). Each scene turns on seeing, and John uses several verbs for it: blepō for Mary seeing the stone removed (verse 1) and the disciple looking in (verse 5), theōreō for Peter gazing at the cloths (verse 6) and Mary seeing the angels and Jesus (verses 12 and 14), and horaō for seeing with understanding, as when the beloved disciple saw and believed (verse 8), Mary announces I have seen the Lord (verse 18), and the disciples tell Thomas the same (verse 25). Some interpreters build too much on the differences between these verbs, but the progression is real: from looking at evidence to recognizing the Lord.

Recognition comes through personal address, not proof alone. Mary does not know Jesus by sight but by his calling her name, echoing the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name (10:3). The disciples know him by his wounds; Thomas is invited to touch them. The scenes also mirror each other: two disciples run to the tomb and one believes (verse 8); Mary weeps and is sent as the first messenger (verse 17); the disciples receive peace, mission, and Spirit; Thomas moves from the strongest refusal in the Gospel (verse 25) to its highest confession (verse 28). That confession forms a frame with the Gospel's opening, which said the Word was God (1:1) and that the only God has made the Father known (1:18). Jesus' final saying in the chapter is one of only two beatitudes in John (the other is 13:17): blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.

John's account overlaps with the others at several points. Luke too tells of Peter running to the tomb and seeing the linen cloths (Luke 24:12) and of Jesus appearing to the disciples in Jerusalem on Easter evening and showing them his wounds (Luke 24:36-43); Matthew tells of Jesus meeting the women on their way from the tomb (Matthew 28:9-10). The Gospels differ in the number of women and angels named and in where the appearances are placed, which each writer arranges for his own purpose. The closing verses (30 and 31) tell the reader that the signs of the whole book were selected, not exhaustive, and were written so that the reader may believe and have life.

outline.t: Peter and the beloved disciple at the empty tomb
Jesus appears to the disciples and breathes the Spirit
Thomas: My Lord and my God

doctrines.note: The resurrection is bodily. The tomb is empty, the grave clothes are left behind, and the risen Jesus shows the marks of the nails and invites Thomas to touch them (verses 20 and 27), yet he is changed, standing among the disciples behind locked doors. The church confesses his bodily resurrection as the firstfruits and pattern of the resurrection of all who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:20).

Thomas calls Jesus “My Lord and my God!” (verse 28), and Jesus accepts it. The Gospel that began by saying the Word was God and became flesh (1:1, 1:14) reaches its climax with a disciple confessing the risen man, wounds and all, as God. The risen Lord remains fully human, bearing the marks of the cross, and is worshiped as God.

Jesus breathes on the disciples and says “Receive the Holy Spirit” (verse 22). The verb echoes God breathing life into the first human (Genesis 2:7) and the breath entering the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9), and it fulfills the promises of the Advocate who would come once Jesus was glorified (7:39, 16:7). How this giving relates to Pentecost is discussed below.

“As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you” (verse 21). The church's mission is modeled on Jesus' own, sent by the Father in love to the world (3:16-17), and it is empowered by the Spirit he gives. The authority to declare sins forgiven or retained (verse 23) belongs to that mission of bearing witness to the gospel, however the churches have ordered its exercise.

John writes “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (verse 31). Faith is not wishful thinking but trust based on testimony. The beloved disciple believes on the evidence of the empty tomb, Mary on hearing her name, Thomas on seeing the wounds, and later readers on the written witness of those who saw; Jesus pronounces them blessed (verse 29).

words.note: Pisteuō, to believe, trust, entrust oneself. It occurs about 241 times in the New Testament and 98 times in John, while the noun pistis, faith, never appears in the Gospel at all, as though faith is always something done. In this chapter the beloved disciple believes (verse 8), Thomas refuses to believe (verse 25) and then believes (verse 29), and the book's purpose is that the reader believe and have life (verse 31). Believing in John means more than accepting facts; it means entrusting oneself to Jesus. In verse 27 Jesus tells Thomas not to be apistos but pistos, literally unbelieving but believing, a word play the BSB renders ‘Stop doubting and believe’.

Emphusaō, to breathe on or into, occurs only here in the New Testament. The Greek Old Testament uses it for God breathing the breath of life into the first human (Genesis 2:7), for the breath that enters the slain in Ezekiel's valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9), and in Wisdom 15:11 for the one who breathed a living spirit into humanity. The echo suggests a new creation: on the first day of the week, in a Gospel that began In the beginning, the risen Jesus breathes the life of the Spirit into his people.

Anistēmi, to rise, stand up, raise. It occurs about 108 times in the New Testament, often simply of standing up, and in John 6:39-54 and 11:23-24 of the raising of the dead at the last day. In verse 9 it is the word for Jesus' rising from the dead, which the disciples had not yet understood from the Scripture that it was necessary (dei). The same verb is used in Acts for Jesus' resurrection (Acts 2:24, 2:32). It describes the dead being raised to bodily life, not merely surviving as spirits.

Haptō, in the middle voice to touch, take hold of, cling to. It occurs about 39 times in the New Testament, often of Jesus touching the sick. In verse 17 Jesus' words mē mou haptou use a present imperative with a negative, which usually means stop doing something already in progress: stop holding on to me. The traditional Latin, Noli me tangere, and the KJV's ‘Touch me not’ have led some to think Jesus forbade any touch, but he invites Thomas to touch him a week later. The reason he gives is that he has not yet ascended; Mary must not cling to the old way of having him but go and tell the others.

Apostellō, to send out on a mission, occurs about 132 times in the New Testament and 28 times in John, most often of the Father sending the Son (3:17, 17:18). In verse 21 Jesus uses it for the Father sending him and the related verb pempō for his sending of the disciples. John uses the two verbs largely interchangeably, as most commentators judge, so the point is not a difference between them but the pattern: the disciples' mission is modeled on and derived from the Son's. The noun apostolos, one sent, comes from this verb.

Aphiēmi, to let go, release, leave, and of sins, to forgive. It occurs about 143 times in the New Testament. BDAG lists the sense of canceling a debt or releasing someone from guilt. In verse 23 it is paired with krateō, to hold fast, retain. The forms are notable: the forgiven sins are said in the best manuscripts to have been forgiven (a perfect passive), which some interpreters take to mean that the disciples declare what God has already done, while others note that the perfect need not carry that weight. The saying parallels the binding and loosing of Matthew 16:19 and 18:18.

Kurios, lord, master, sir, and in the Greek Old Testament the regular substitute for the divine name YHWH. It occurs about 717 times in the New Testament. In this chapter Mary calls the gardener kurie, sir (verse 15), speaks of my Lord (verses 2 and 13), and announces I have seen the Lord (verse 18). Thomas's confession, My Lord and my God (verse 28), joins kurios with theos in the way the Greek Psalms address Israel's God, and shows the word moving from courtesy to worship within a single chapter.

Eirēnē, peace, occurs about 92 times in the New Testament and 6 times in John. In Greek it could mean simply the absence of war, but in the Bible it carries the fullness of the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, right relationship, and well-being given by God. Jesus had promised to leave his peace with the disciples, not as the world gives (14:27), and said that in him they would have peace though in the world they would have trouble (16:33). Three times in this chapter the risen Jesus says “Peace be with you,” a greeting that becomes a gift.

christ:
This chapter shows that the crucified Jesus is alive in the body, the same person with the same wounds, now raised beyond death. He calls Mary by name as the good shepherd calls his sheep, gives peace to disciples who failed him, shows them the marks of his suffering, sends them as he was sent, and breathes the Spirit into them. He speaks of “My Father and your Father, to My God and your God” (verse 17), and for the first time calls the disciples his brothers: his death and resurrection have drawn his followers into his own relationship with the Father, fulfilling the promise that those who receive him become children of God (1:12). He is still distinct from them (my Father and your Father, not our Father), for he is the Son by nature and they are sons and daughters by grace.

The risen Jesus is the beginning of the new creation. He is raised on the first day of the week, found in a garden, and breathes life into a new humanity, and many readers see the whole Gospel's opening echo, In the beginning, answered here. Scripture had pointed to this, as verse 9 says, though John does not name the texts. In Acts, Peter cites Psalm 16, where the Lord's holy one does not see decay (Acts 2:25-31), and Isaiah 53 had spoken of the servant who, after being cut off, would see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53:10-11).

Thomas's confession is the high point of the Gospel's teaching about who Jesus is: he is Lord and God. The book that began with the Word who was with God and was God (1:1) now shows a Jewish disciple, raised to worship the one God of Israel, bowing before the risen Jesus with Israel's words for God. Jesus accepts the worship. For the church this is the center of the faith; as Paul says, “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). John sets the testimony of eyewitnesses in writing precisely so that people who were not there can believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name.
interpretation:
The earliest Jewish response to the Easter proclamation is recorded by Christians: the story that the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:11-15), still circulating in Justin Martyr's day (Dialogue with Trypho 108). The medieval Toledot Yeshu tells of a gardener who hid the body, a detail that may play on Mary's mistake in verse 15. Modern Jewish scholars have taken the question seriously: Pinchas Lapide argued that the disciples' transformation required a real event, and Geza Vermes (The Resurrection, 2008) surveyed the explanations and found none fully satisfying while declining the Christian conclusion.

Among the fathers, Augustine (Tractates on John 121) said that Thomas saw and touched a man and confessed the God he could neither see nor touch. Gregory the Great, in a homily on this chapter (Homilies on the Gospels 26, 591), taught that Thomas's unbelief did more for our faith than the faith of the believing disciples, because his touching the wounds heals the wounds of our doubt. Gregory also, in another homily of the same series, identified Mary Magdalene with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and with Mary of Bethany, a conflation that shaped Western art for over a thousand years; the Eastern church never made it. Thomas Aquinas called Mary Magdalene the apostle of the apostles because she was sent to announce the resurrection to them. In 2016 the Roman Catholic Church raised her memorial on 22 July to a feast, citing that title.

Verses 22 and 23 have been contested for centuries. Theodore of Mopsuestia treated the breathing as a symbolic promise of the Spirit to be given at Pentecost. Augustine (On the Trinity, book 4) cited it as evidence that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father, a text used in the Western defense of the filioque, the phrase and the Son added to the Nicene Creed in the West. At the Reformation, the Augsburg Confession (1530, article 28) tied the power of the keys to preaching the gospel, forgiving and retaining sins, and administering the sacraments, while the Council of Trent (session 14, 1551, canon 3) condemned those who deny that these words refer to the power of forgiving sins in the sacrament of penance.

In art, Fra Angelico painted Noli me tangere in a friar's cell at San Marco in Florence (1440 to 1441), and Titian's version (about 1514) is in the National Gallery, London. Caravaggio's The Incredulity of Saint Thomas (about 1601 to 1602, now at Sanssouci in Potsdam) shows Jesus guiding Thomas's finger into the wound, though the text never says Thomas actually touched him. In the liturgy, verses 1 to 18 are read on Easter Day in the Revised Common Lectionary, and verses 19 to 31 on the Second Sunday of Easter in all three years; the Orthodox call that day Thomas Sunday, and since 2000 the Roman Catholic Church has kept it as Divine Mercy Sunday. Modern critical study has compared John's account with the other Gospels' in detail, and theologians such as Wolfhart Pannenberg (Jesus: God and Man, 1964) argued that the resurrection must be treated as a historical claim open to investigation, not only as an article of faith.
text:
The most significant manuscript difference in the chapter is in verse 31. The earliest witnesses divide between a present subjunctive, pisteuēte, that you may keep on believing (found in P66 as far as it can be read, the first hand of Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus), and an aorist, pisteusēte, that you may come to believe (in the later corrector of Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Bezae, and most later manuscripts). The first reading suggests a book written to strengthen believers, the second a book written to bring readers to faith. Many scholars prefer the present as the harder reading, but the difference should not be pressed: in Greek of this period the aorist and present subjunctive can both be used for coming to faith and continuing in it, and John's book does both.

In verse 16 the words ‘in Hebrew’ (that is, in Aramaic) are absent from the Byzantine manuscripts behind the King James Version. In verse 23 the manuscripts vary between the present tense aphientai, they are forgiven, and the perfect apheōntai, they have been forgiven; modern editions print the perfect. In verse 29 the King James Version begins Jesus' words with ‘Thomas’, following later manuscripts.

Translation differences are more visible. In verse 17 the KJV's ‘Touch me not’ reflects the Latin Noli me tangere; modern versions, reading the present imperative, say ‘Do not cling to Me’ (BSB, ESV) or ‘Do not hold on to me’ (NIV). In verse 27 the KJV's ‘be not faithless, but believing’ keeps the Greek word play; the BSB paraphrases ‘Stop doubting and believe’ and the ESV says ‘Do not disbelieve, but believe’. In verse 1 the first day of the week renders a Greek idiom, literally ‘one of the sabbaths’, in which sabbath means week.

teach.big: The crucified Jesus is bodily risen, and he meets grieving, frightened, and doubting people personally, gives them peace and his Spirit, and sends them out, so that those who have not seen may believe and have life.

outline.t: Easter begins in darkness and misunderstanding: the first witness assumes the worst, and the risen Lord meets her anyway.
The evidence of the empty tomb and orderly grave clothes leads one disciple to faith, even before he understands the Scriptures.
Jesus meets Mary in her grief, calls her by name, and makes a woman the first messenger of the resurrection to the apostles.
The risen Lord brings peace to those who failed him, shows his wounds, gives the Spirit, and sends his people as he was sent.
Jesus answers honest doubt with evidence and invitation, and Thomas's doubt becomes the Gospel's highest confession: My Lord and my God.
The Gospel was written with a purpose: that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats the resurrection as a metaphor for new hope or spiritual renewal. John insists on a body that can be seen, heard, touched, and recognized by its wounds; the church confesses a bodily resurrection. The opposite error treats the chapter as a courtroom proof that should compel belief. John offers testimony, and even the disciples needed more than evidence: Mary needed her name spoken, and the beloved disciple believed before he understood.

A second misreading makes Thomas a villain. He is honest, he states his conditions openly, and Jesus meets him without contempt; his confession surpasses all the others. The label doubting Thomas can shame people who ask real questions. A third ignores Mary Magdalene's role or repeats the medieval claim that she was a reformed prostitute, which the text never says. A fourth reads verse 23 narrowly through a single church's practice without acknowledging that Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, and free-church traditions interpret the authority to forgive and retain sins differently. A fifth treats verse 22 and Pentecost as a contradiction to be explained away quickly; it is better to present the main readings fairly.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks to the grieving: Mary weeps at a grave and is met by name, and those who have stood at a tomb will hear that. It speaks to those who carry doubt, especially people who fear that asking questions disqualifies them; Jesus comes back for Thomas. It speaks to those who have failed and are hiding in fear, as the disciples were. Teach it with care for people whose grief is recent, without rushing them past the tears Mary was allowed to shed, and without making resurrection hope sound like a denial of loss.

hard.q: Did Jesus really rise from the dead, and can the Gospel accounts be trusted when they differ?
hard.a:
The objection has several parts, and each has capable defenders. The philosophical part goes back to David Hume (An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, 1748, section 10), who argued that no testimony can make a miracle more likely than the uniform experience of nature against it. The historical part points to differences among the Easter accounts: how many women went to the tomb, whether there were one or two angels, and whether the appearances were in Jerusalem (Luke, John 20) or Galilee (Matthew, Mark's promise, John 21). Hermann Samuel Reimarus, in fragments published by Gotthold Lessing in the 1770s, pressed such contradictions as evidence of invention. Modern critics offer natural explanations: Gerd Lüdemann (The Resurrection of Jesus, 1994) proposed grief and guilt visions, beginning with Peter; John Dominic Crossan doubted that Jesus had an identifiable tomb; and Bart Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014) argued that the disciples sincerely had visions but that the empty tomb stories are later. On these views the resurrection is a belief the disciples came to hold, not an event that happened to Jesus.

The responses are also several. Against Hume, C. S. Lewis (Miracles, 1947) and others argued that the argument assumes nature is closed to God, which is the very question at issue; if God exists and raised Jesus, the event would be unique by definition. On the history, N. T. Wright (The Resurrection of the Son of God, 2003) argued that the disciples' belief, their redefinition of resurrection, their worship of Jesus, and the move to Sunday worship require both an empty tomb and meetings with Jesus to explain them. Dale Allison (Resurrecting Jesus, 2005), who does not claim to settle the question, still judged both the empty tomb and the appearances to be likely historical. Pinchas Lapide, a Jewish scholar, judged that only a real event could explain the disciples' change. On the differences between the Gospels, many point out that independent witnesses routinely differ in detail while agreeing on the core, and that all four agree on the essentials: women first at the tomb, early on the first day, the tomb empty, the risen Jesus meeting his followers. The church confesses the bodily resurrection as the ground of its faith; those who do not share that faith will weigh the same evidence through different assumptions about what is possible, and the argument often turns on those assumptions.

hard.q: Jesus gives the Holy Spirit here (20:22), but Acts says the Spirit came at Pentecost. How do these fit together?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real. Acts says Jesus told the disciples to wait in Jerusalem until they were clothed with power from on high, and that the Spirit was poured out on the day of Pentecost, fifty days after Passover (Luke 24:49, Acts 1:4-8, 2:1-4). John places a giving of the Spirit on Easter evening. Some critical scholars conclude that the two writers simply preserve different traditions of when and how the Spirit came, and that they should not be harmonized; the scene is often called the Johannine Pentecost, and Raymond Brown's commentary treats it as John's counterpart to Luke's account, his own telling of the same gift.

Other interpreters see two stages. Theodore of Mopsuestia and, among modern commentators, D. A. Carson (The Gospel According to John, 1991) read the breathing as an acted promise, a sign of the gift that would be given at Pentecost. John Chrysostom (Homilies on John 86) held that the disciples received a real grace on Easter evening, especially the authority to forgive sins, and the fuller gifts of power at Pentecost. A third view distinguishes the Spirit given for new life and forgiveness, as the breath of new creation in John, from the Spirit given as power for public witness in Acts; this reading is common in Pentecostal and many evangelical traditions. Each view has its strength: the first respects the distinct voices of John and Luke, the second and third take seriously that both describe real events.

What both writers agree on is that the Spirit is the gift of the risen and exalted Jesus, that he is given to send the church into the world, and that the church cannot bear witness without him. The question of exact timing is second-order, and readers across traditions hold these views in good faith.

observe: What does each person see at the tomb in verses 1 to 8, and who is said to believe?
What three things does Jesus give or do for the disciples in verses 19 to 23?
What exactly did Thomas say he needed before he would believe, and what does Jesus offer him?
interpret: Mary recognizes Jesus only when he says her name. What does this suggest about how the risen Christ makes himself known?
Why do you think Jesus shows his wounds rather than appearing without them? What do the wounds say about who the risen Jesus is?
Verse 31 says the book was written so that you may believe. How does knowing the author's purpose shape how you read the rest of the Gospel?
apply: Thomas wanted evidence, and Jesus met him with it. How can honesty about doubt and trust in testimony belong together in your own faith?
Jesus sends his disciples as the Father sent him. What would it look like for you to be sent into the places where you already live and work?
When you weigh the witness of this chapter, what do you find most and least persuasive, and why?
